claims.text: Introducing a functionally graded RHEA interlayer between W and CuCrZr will lower thermal stress relative to a single-material interlayer or direct bond.
Introducing a functionally graded RHEA interlayer between W and CuCrZr will reduce interfacial cracking under fusion-relevant thermal cycling.
The proposed interlayer transitions compositionally from a Cu-rich region to a W-based region.
Powder-metallurgy-related methods can be used to manufacture RHEAs.
Advanced powder metallurgy or additive manufacturing can fabricate the proposed Cu-rich-to-W-based graded RHEA interlayer.
Fusion plasma-facing components are expected to operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K.
An inert or low-oxidation environment is representative of service conditions for the proposed fusion-reactor joint.
The structural mediator is a gradated interlayer progressing from Cu-rich material through RHEA content to a W-based region.
Gradual compositional changes minimize abrupt thermal-expansion mismatch at the W–CuCrZr interface.
Reducing abrupt thermal-expansion mismatch distributes thermomechanical stress through the graded interlayer.
Distributing thermomechanical stress mitigates delamination during cyclic heating.
The graded interlayer will produce lower crack density, higher shear strength, and reduced interfacial stress than the control joints.
The graded interlayer will improve interfacial longevity and stability.
Pure-Cu, Ni, or direct W-to-CuCrZr joints exhibit higher thermal stress and premature interfacial failure during cycling.
Excessive interlayer thickness may foster brittle phases.
Suboptimal RHEA compositions may foster brittle phases.
Long-term service of the graded W–RHEA–CuCrZr joint requires validation under irradiation and full reactor conditions.
The effects of local compositional variation and possible phase separation in the proposed gradient are insufficiently characterized for long-term service.
RHEAs generally possess promising elevated-temperature mechanical properties and thermal stability for hostile or nuclear environments.
